'''''Allocasuarina torulosa''''', commonly known as '''forest oak''', '''rose sheoak''',<ref name="foa">{{cite web |title=''Allocasuarina torulosa'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Allocasuarina%20torulosa |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of Agriculture, Water and the Environment: Canberra |access-date=18 August 2023}}</ref> '''river oak''' or '''Baker's oak''',<ref name="RFK">{{cite web |author1=F.A.Zich |author2=B.P.M.Hyland |author3=T.Whiffen |author4=R.A.Kerrigan |author2-link=Bernard Hyland |year=2020 |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/rainforest/text/entities/Allocasuarina_torulosa.htm |title=''Allocasuarina torulosa'' |website=[[Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants]] Edition 8 (RFK8) |publisher=Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research (CANBR), [[Australian Government]] |access-date=24 June 2021}}</ref> is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Casuarinaceae]] and is [[endemic]] to eastern Australia. It is a slender, usually [[Dioecy|dioecious]] tree that has drooping branchlets up to {{cvt|140|mm}} long, the leaves reduced to scales in whorls of four or five, and the fruiting cones {{cvt|15–33|mm|sigfig=1}} long containing winged seeds ([[Samara (fruit)|samaras]]) {{cvt|7–10|mm|sigfig=1}} long.

==Description==
''Allocasuarina torulosa'' is a slender, usually dioecious tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|5–20|m}}. Its branchlets are drooping, up to {{cvt|140|mm}} long, the leaves reduced to erect, scale-like teeth {{cvt|0.3–0.8|mm|sigfig=1}} long, arranged in whorls of four or five around the branchlets. The sections of branchlet between the leaf whorls are {{cvt|5–6|mm|sigfig=2}} long, {{cvt|0.4–0.5|mm|sigfig=2}} wide and more or less square in cross-section when young. Male flowers are arranged in spikes {{cvt|5–30|mm|sigfig=1}} long, with 7 to 12 whorls per cm (per 0.4 in), the [[Stamen#Morphology and terminology|anthers]] {{cvt|0.5–0.6|mm|sigfig=2}} long. Fruiting cones are on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|8–30|mm|sigfig=1}} long, and mature [[infructescence]]s (fuiting cones) are warty, shortly cylindrical to barrel-shaped, {{cvt|15–33|mm|sigfig=1}} long and {{cvt|12–25|mm|sigfig=1}} in diameter, containing brown, winged seeds ([[Samara (fruit)|samaras]]) {{cvt|7–10|mm|sigfig=1}} long.<ref name="foa" /><ref name="RFK" /><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Wilson |first1=Karen L. |last2=Johnson |first2=Lawrence A.S. |title=''Allocasuarina torulosa'' |url=https://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Allocasuarina~torulosa |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=18 August 2023}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
Forest oak was first formally described in 1789 by [[William Aiton]], who gave it the name ''Casuarina torulosa'' in ''[[Hortus Kewensis]]'' from specimens collected by [[Joseph Banks]].<ref name=APNI1>{{cite web|title=''Casuarina torulosa''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/459378|publisher=APNI|access-date=18 August 2023}}</ref><ref name="Aiton">{{cite book |last1=Aiton |first1=William |title=Hortus Kewensis |volume=3 |date=1789 |location=London |page=320 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/23434#page/323/mode/1up |access-date=18 August 2023}}</ref> In 1982, [[Lawrence Alexander Sidney Johnson|Lawrie Johnson]] transferred the species to ''Allocasuarina'' as ''A. torulosa'' in the ''[[Journal of the Adelaide Botanic Gardens]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Allocasuarina torulosa''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/499448|publisher=APNI|access-date=18 August 2023}}</ref><ref name="JABG">{{cite journal |last1=Johnson |first1=Lawrence A.S. |title=Notes on Casuarinaceae II. |journal=Journal of the Adelaide Botanic Gardens |date=1982 |volume=6 |issue=1 |page=78 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/61978679#page/90/mode/1up |access-date=5 August 2023}}</ref> Since it was the first species of the genus ''Allocasuarina'' to be named by Johnson, it is the [[type species]] of that genus.<ref name=APNItype>{{cite web|title=''Allocasuarina''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/499181|publisher=APNI|access-date=18 August 2023}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Allocasuarina torulosa'' grows in open forest and on rainforest fringes in moister, more nutrient rich soils than ''[[Allocasuarina littoralis|A. littoralis]]'' at altitudes from {{cvt|40 to 1200|m}}. It is widespread in north-eastern and central-eastern Queensland and on the coast and ranges of New South Wales, as far south as [[Macquarie Pass]] and [[Jenolan Caves]]. There is also an isolated population on [[Cape York Peninsula]].<ref name="foa" /><ref name="RFK" /><ref name="RBGS" />

==Uses==
The timber is reddish pink to brown.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Rose sheoak {{!}} The Wood Database - Lumber Identification (Hardwood)|url=https://www.wood-database.com/rose-sheoak/|access-date=2021-04-26|language=en-US}}</ref> The rose she-oak has the largest contraction along the grain (12%) of any Australian wood and needs to be dried carefully to get full value as a useful timber.<ref>{{Cite web|title=She-Oaks in a Rural Landscape|url=https://glossyblack.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Fact-Sheet-2-Living-with-Glossy-Blacks-She-oaks-in-a-rural-landscape.pdf|url-status=live|access-date=April 26, 2021|website=Glossy Black Conservancy|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190226201703/https://glossyblack.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2017/06/Fact-Sheet-2-Living-with-Glossy-Blacks-She-oaks-in-a-rural-landscape.pdf |archive-date=26 February 2019 }}</ref>

==Ecology==
The seeds of ''A. torulosa'' have been found to be a food source for the [[yellow-tailed black cockatoo]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=''Allocasuarina torulosa'' |url=http://plantselector.botanicgardens.sa.gov.au/Plants/Details/775|access-date=2021-04-26|website=plantselector.botanicgardens.sa.gov.au}}</ref>

==Use in horticulture==
It grows from [[seed]],<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Stewart|first=Angus|title=Allocasuarina torulosa -- Forest she-oak|url=https://www.gardeningwithangus.com.au/allocasuarina-torulosa-forest-she-oak/|url-status=live|access-date=April 26, 2021|website=Gardening with Angus|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200921033028/https://www.gardeningwithangus.com.au/allocasuarina-torulosa-forest-she-oak/ |archive-date=21 September 2020 }}</ref> and cut or broken trees will often regenerate from the trunk.

This is a low-maintenance tree that will grow in a variety of soils and tolerate light frosts.<ref name=":2" /> In the [[United States|USA]], it is suitable for [[Hardiness zone|USDA hardiness zones]] 8–11. It may be susceptible to [[Armillaria]] and [[Phytophthora]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=UFEI - SelecTree: A Tree Selection Guide|url=https://selectree.calpoly.edu/tree-detail/allocasuarina-torulosa|access-date=2021-04-26|website=selectree.calpoly.edu}}</ref>
